Oxidation states 
By definition, the oxidation state of any atom in an elementary substance 
is zero. In compounds and ions, some elements have constant oxidation 
states (table 7). 
V¥ Table 7 Elements with constant oxidation states in compounds and ions 
Element Oxidation state 
group 1 metals (Li, Na, K, Rb and Cs) +1 
group 2 metals (Be, Mg, Ca, Srand Ba) +2 
early group 13 elements (B and Al) +3 
fluorine (F) -1 
For other elements, the oxidation states are assigned according to the 
following rules. 
* Hydrogen has an oxidation state of +1 when bonded to a non-metal 
(e.g. in HCI) but -1 when bonded to a metal (e.g. in NaH). 
* Oxygen has an oxidation state of -2 except in peroxides (species with an 
—0-0- linkage) and compounds with fluorine. 
* Halogens (Cl, Br and I) have an oxidation state of -1 unless they form 
bonds with fluorine or oxygen. 
* The sum of the oxidation states of all the atoms in a molecule is zero. 
* The sum of the oxidation states of all the atoms in a polyatomic ion equals 
the charge of that ion. 
Transition metals and most main group non-metals have variable oxidation 
states. These states are specified by Roman numerals. For example, the 
systematic names for FeCl, and SO, are iron(I1I) chloride and sulfur(IV) oxide, 
respectively. In traditional names of oxoanions, such as sulfate (SO,*) and 
sulfite (SOBZ‘), the oxidation states of the central atoms are omitted.

The activity series 
The activity series, also known as the electrochemical series, ranks metals in 
order of the ease of their oxidation, and enables you to predict whether 
certain redox reactions will occur or not. More active metals displace less 
active metals from their compounds, for example: 
Fe(s) + CuSO,(aq) — FeSO,(aq) + Cu(s) (molecular equation) 
Fe(s) + Cu?*(aq) — Fe**(aq) + Cu(s) (net ionic equation) 
Similarly, more active halogens displace less active halogens, for example: 
2KBr(aq) + CL(g) — 2KCl(aq) + Br,(aq) (molecular equation) 
2Br(aq) + Cl(g) — 2Cl(aq) + Br (aq) (net ionic equation) 
In contrast, the reverse reactions do not proceed spontaneously. 
All metals above hydrogen in the activity series react with non-oxidizing acids, 
such as hydrochloric acid and dilute sulfuric acid, to produce metal salts and 
hydrogen gas, for example: 
Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) — ZnCl (aq) + H (g) (molecular equation) 
Zn(s) + 2H*(aq) — Zn**(aq) + H(g) (net ionic equation)

Electrochemical cells 
Electrochemical cells interconvert chemical and electrical energy via redox 
reactions. Voltaic cells, also known as galvanic cells, use the chemical energy 
of spontaneous redox reactions to produce electrical energy. In electrolytic 
cells, the electrical energy from an external source is used to bring about 
non-spontaneous chemical reactions. 
* Electrochemical cells interconvert chemical and electrical energy. 
* Voltaic (galvanic) cells generate electricity from spontaneous redox 
reactions. 
* Electrolytic cells use electricity to force non-spontaneous redox 
reactions to occur. 
In a voltaic cell, the two parts of a redox reaction, the oxidation and reduction 
processes, occur in two separate half-cells, each containing an electrode 
and an electrolyte solution. The electrodes are connected by a wire and the 
solutions are connected by a salt bridge to complete the circuit (figure 4). 
This separation prevents the spontaneous reaction from occurring in a single 
half-cell and forces the electrons to travel through the wire while ions move 
through the salt bridge. The electricity produced by the cell can be detected 
by a voltmeter or used to power a light bulb or any other electrical device.

In all electrochemical cells, reduction occurs at the cathode, and oxidation at 
the anode. In voltaic cells, one species spontaneously undergoes reduction 
and withdraws electrons from the cathode, making it positive. At the same 
time, another species undergoes oxidation and releases electrons to the 
anode, making it negative. In electrolytic cells, the polarity of electrodes is 
reversed (table 8).

Cell diagrams, also known as cell notation, are a shorthand way to represent 
voltaic cells. By convention, the cathode is always shown on the right-hand 
side, and the anode on the left-hand side. The boundaries between electrodes 
and electrolytes are represented by single vertical lines, and the salt bridge by 
a double vertical line. For example, the diagram for the Daniell cell in figure 4 
would be written as follows: 
Zn(s) | Zn*(aq) || Cu*(aq) | Cu(s) 
Voltaic cells are classified as primary cells (non-rechargeable), secondary cells 
(rechargeable) and fuel cells (table 9). Primary cells can be used only once 
because the redox processes in these cells cannot be reversed. In contrast, 
secondary cells can be recharged using external power sources. Fuel cells can 
work continuously for as long as fuel is supplied.

During the electrolysis, electrons from the DC power source flow to the 
cathode and reduce the cations in the electrolyte. The anions in the electrolyte 
flow to the anode and undergo oxidation, releasing electrons. These electrons 
flow to the DC power source to complete the circuit. 
Lead can be produced by the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide, 
PbBr(1). 
a) Explain how molten lead(II) bromide conducts electricity. 
b) State half-equations for the reactions occurring at the electrodes. 
c) Deduce the overall cell reaction. 
d) Outline what you would observe during the electrolysis. 
e) Outline the hazards associated with this experiment and the safety 
precautions that must be taken when carrying it out. 
Solution 
a) Lead(IT) bromide contains ions that are free to move only in the molten 
state. The Pb* ions are positively charged, so they move towards the 
negative electrode (cathode). The Br-ions are negatively charged, so 
they move towards the positive electrode (anode). 
b) Reduction (cathode): Pb** + 2e~ — Pb(l) 
Oxidation (anode): 2Br- — Br,(g) + 2e" 
Notice that, at high temperature, lead metal will be liquid and bromine 
will be gaseous. 
c) Overall cell reaction: PbBr,(1) — Pb(1) + Br,(g) 
d) Asilvery-grey molten metal, Pb(1), will form at the cathode, and a 
brown gas with a characteristic odour will form at the anode, Brz(g). 
e) Bromine is both corrosive and toxic. Lead(II) bromide is toxic. Molten 
saltis hot, and it might splatter during the electrolysis. The experiment 
must be carried out in a fume cupboard. A face shield, protective 
gloves and laboratory coat must be used.

Active electrodes can also be used for purifying metals by electrolytic refining. 
An impure metal, such as raw copper, is oxidized at the anode and reduced at 
the cathode. Any impurities present in the raw metal either stay in the solution 
or form a precipitate at the bottom of the electrolytic cell. The process can be 
repeated several times until the metal of desired purity is obtained.

A radical is a chemical entity, typically an atom or molecule, that has an 
unpaired electron. This electron is commonly shown as a dot (+). For example, 
chlorine and methyl radicals are represented as Cl- and -CH,, respectively. 
Radicals are formed by homolytic fission of covalent bonds, which involves 
the breaking of the bonding electron pair and the movement of individual 
electrons in opposite directions. In reaction mechanisms, this type of electron 
movement is shown by single-barbed (fish-hook) arrows (figure 8). 
clric — cr + cr 
A Figure 8 Homolytic fission of chlorine, Clz, to form chlorine radicals, Cl￾Due to their high reactivity, radicals are usually formed in chemical reactions as 
intermediates rather than final products. 
Radical substitution in alkanes 
At low temperatures, alkanes are relatively unreactive because all C—C and 
C—H bonds in their molecules are strong and almost non-polar. However, 
alkanes participate in radical substitution (SR) reactions with halogens. These 
reactions are initiated by ultraviolet (UV) light or heat and involve initiation, 
propagation and termination steps.
